1-1.text: Part one. Day and night. ... The Earth is a giant ball that spins. It spins round its axis: an imaginary line through the North Pole and the South Pole.

1-2.text: The half of the Earth facing the Sun has day. The half facing away is in shadow: that's night.

1-3.text: The Earth spins round once in about 24 hours. That gives us one day and one night.

1-4.text: The Sun isn't moving round us. It only seems to cross the sky because the Earth turns. It rises in the east and sets in the west.

2-1.text: Part two. Years and seasons. ... As it spins, the Earth also travels round the Sun. One trip, called an orbit, takes about 365 and a quarter days. That's one year.

2-2.text: The quarter days add up. So every four years we add an extra day, the 29th of February. That's a leap year.

2-3.text: The Earth's axis is tilted. As the Earth goes round the Sun, the axis always leans the same way.

2-4.text: In June the UK leans towards the Sun. The Sun climbs high in the sky and the days are long. It's summer.

2-5.text: In December the UK leans away from the Sun. The Sun stays low and the days are short. It's winter.

3-1.text: Part three. The Solar System. ... At the centre of our Solar System is the Sun. The Sun is a star: a huge ball of very hot, glowing gas.

3-2.text: Eight planets orbit the Sun. In order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

3-3.text: A silly sentence helps you remember the order: My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming.

3-4.text: The four inner planets are small and rocky. The four outer planets are giants, made mostly of gas and ice.

3-5.text: Planets further from the Sun take longer to go round. The Earth takes one year, but Neptune takes about 165 years!

4-1.text: Part four. The Moon. ... The Moon orbits the Earth. One orbit takes about 27 days, roughly a month.

4-2.text: The Moon doesn't make its own light. We see it because it reflects light from the Sun.

4-3.text: The Sun always lights up half of the Moon. As the Moon goes round the Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half.

4-4.text: So the Moon seems to change shape. These shapes are called the phases of the Moon: new moon, crescent, half moon, full moon, and back again.

5-1.text: Part five. Gravity in space. ... Gravity is a pull between any two objects with mass. The bigger the mass, the stronger the pull. It gets weaker further away.

5-2.text: The Sun's gravity keeps the Earth and the other planets in their orbits. The Earth's gravity keeps the Moon in its orbit.

5-3.text: Different worlds have different gravity. It is about 10 newtons per kilogram on the Earth, 1 point 6 newtons per kilogram on the Moon and 25 newtons per kilogram on Jupiter.

5-4.text: An astronaut's mass is 60 kilograms. She weighs 60 times 10, which is 600 newtons, on the Earth, but only 60 times 1 point 6, which is 96 newtons, on the Moon. Her mass is still 60 kilograms.

6-1.text: Part six. Stars and galaxies. ... The Sun is our nearest star. The stars you see at night are suns too, but they are much, much further away.

6-2.text: Light is the fastest thing there is. Even so, light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach us.

6-3.text: Space is so big that we use light years. A light year is a distance: how far light travels in one year.

6-4.text: One light year is about nine and a half million million kilometres. The next nearest star after the Sun is over 4 light years away.

6-5.text: Stars are grouped in huge galaxies. We live in the Milky Way, with hundreds of billions of stars. And there are billions of galaxies!
